title: Padres Edge Brewers 5-3: October 4, 2026 GameRecap, Stats & Highlights – CBS Sports
body:
The San Diego Padres fell to the Milwaukee Brewers 6‑3 on October 4, handing Milwaukee a critical win in the final game of the National League Wild Card series and clinching the Padres’ early exit from the postseason. Milwaukee’s young outfielder Jackson Chourio delivered a decisive two‑run double in the seventh inning, a moment he later linked to a painful lesson learned during his rookie season when he failed to produce in a clutch situation. The victory pushed the Brewers to a 2‑1 series edge, securing their spot in the NLDS and underscoring the depth of a roster that has steadily improved throughout the year.

Milwaukee’s pitching staff set the tone early, with starter Nathan Eovaldi (5‑2, 3.11 ERA) dispatching the Padres’ lineup over six innings while allowing just three hits and one run. Eovaldi’s command of the strike zone, highlighted by a mix of high‑velocity fastballs and sharp breaking pitches, forced San Diego’s power hitters—Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado—to swing early and often without much success. The Brewers’ bullpen, anchored by closer Josh Hader, preserved the lead in the final three innings, striking out five and walking none. In contrast, the Padres’ ace, Blake Snell, struggled to find his rhythm, surrendering three runs on five hits in just 4 ⅔ innings, a performance that left San Diego trailing and unable to mount a comeback.

The offensive narrative belonged to Chourio, whose 22‑year‑old breakout season has been defined by timely hitting. After a quiet start to the game, he stepped up in the seventh when the Brewers trailed 3‑2. Facing a full count with two outs, Chourio drove a double to left‑center that cleared the infield and allowed two runners to score, flipping the lead permanently. Post‑game, Chourio reflected on a rookie‑year misstep in 2024 when a similar situation ended in a strikeout, saying, “That moment taught me that the pressure is part of the game. I use it as fuel now.” His comment resonated with a Brewers clubhouse that has embraced a culture of resilience after a turbulent 2025 campaign that saw them finish just above .500 before surging in the final months.

San Diego’s offense, which had been prolific all season, was stifled by Milwaukee’s defensive adjustments. The Padres managed only three runs, all coming in the second inning when Tatis Jr. homered off a fastball that slipped past Eovaldi’s glove. The remainder of the game saw the Padres’ hitters swing at pitches outside the zone, a symptom of the Brewers’ aggressive sequencing and the Padres’ inability to adjust to the shifting count. Manager Jayce Tomas, typically praised for his strategic acumen, was forced to make early bullpen moves that left the Padres without their most effective relievers in the later innings.

The series itself has been a tale of two cities. Milwaukee entered the postseason as the fifth seed, having clinched the Wild Card with a 92‑70 record, while San Diego, a wild‑card entrant themselves, boasted a 95‑67 ledger and a reputation for late‑season surges. The Brewers’ ability to win two of three games against a team that led the NL in runs scored this year highlights the unpredictable nature of playoff baseball, where pitching depth and clutch hitting often outweigh regular‑season statistics.

Looking ahead, the Brewers now turn their focus to the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves, a team that has demonstrated both power and poise throughout the postseason. For the Padres, the loss marks a premature end to a campaign that promised a deep run, prompting front‑office discussions about roster tweaks—particularly in the bullpen—to address the shortcomings exposed by Milwaukee’s disciplined pitching. As the postseason unfolds, Milwaukee’s blend of veteran steadiness and youthful exuberance, epitomized by Chourio’s redemption narrative, positions them as a dark horse capable of upsetting higher‑seeded opponents on their path to the World Series.
